ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Random suffix intercept removed — must know language-as-fixed-effect fallacy
ground_truth.original_snippet: We included two random intercepts, one for subjects and one for suffixes. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject) + (1|suffix), data, family = "binomial").
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").
ground_truth.description: Removed random intercept for suffixes — 'language as fixed effect fallacy' (Clark, 1973); ignores suffix-level clustering, inflating Type I error

matched_finding.subcategory: Experiment 1 model omits item or suffix clustering
matched_finding.description: Experiment 1 model omits item or suffix clustering: The Experiment 1 model appears under-specified for the structure of the data. Responses are clustered not only by participant but also by nonword item and by suffix, while the key predictors are properties of suffixes/items. Without item or suffix random effects, the trial-level model may overstate the precision of the condition and diagnosticity effects, especially for the graded diagnosticity analyses that depend on variation across only 20 suffixes, or 10 suffixes in the separate category-specific analyses.
matched_finding.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the Ime4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points ( $11.7 \%$ of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response). The analysis considered the impact of suffix condition (adjective or noun suffix) on the binomial response (adjective or noun). We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response $\sim$ condition + ( 1 |subject), data, family $=$ "binomial").

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Formula now computes P(suffix|category) not P(category|suffix) — denominator mismatch with definition
ground_truth.original_snippet: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words that contain the suffix.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.
ground_truth.description: Changed denominator from P(category|suffix) to P(suffix|category) — this IS specificity, not diagnosticity; collapses the paper's central theoretical distinction

matched_finding.subcategory: Diagnosticity denominator in the Method section
matched_finding.description: Diagnosticity denominator in the Method section: The type diagnosticity definition appears to use the wrong denominator. As written, it describes $P(\text{suffix} \mid \text{category})$, but the conceptual definition, examples (-TUDE = 1; -IAN = 0.54), token formula, and Appendix A values indicate that diagnosticity is intended as $P(\text{category} \mid \text{suffix})$.
matched_finding.quote: We define diagnosticity as the strength with which a suffix spelling predicts lexical category. For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category. Diagnosticity is thus expressed as a ratio ranging from 0 to 1 . For example, -NIK is not diagnostic for adjectives (diagnosticity is 0 ), whereas -TUDE unambiguously signals a noun (diagnosticity is 1). A suffix like -IAN is present in nouns (magician), as well as in other categories (Amazonian), and so is not particularly diagnostic for nouns (type diagnosticity of 0.54 ).

matched_finding.subcategory: Pretarget word-count imbalance may affect key eye measures
matched_finding.description: Pretarget word-count imbalance may affect key eye measures: The significant pre-target word-count imbalance is a potential confound for go-past time and regressions-out, because these measures can include or be triggered by regressions into the pre-target region. Although pre-target letters were matched and the difference is small, the analysis as described does not show that the congruency effects survive controlling for pre-target word count or related sentence-frame properties.
matched_finding.quote: Sentence parts preceding targets were matched across conditions on the number of letters (congruent: 30.48 letters on average, incongruent: 31.70 letters, $p>0.3$ ). Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, $\mathrm{t}(64)=2.07, \mathrm{p}<0.05$ ). Post-target contexts were matched on the number of letters ( 25.02 vs 26.33 , respectively, $\mathrm{p}>0.05$ ) and the number of words ( 4.38 vs 4.56 , respectively, $\mathrm{p}>0.05$ ). Pretarget words were always at least five characters long (with no difference across conditions: $7.33 \mathrm{vs} 7.15, \mathrm{p}>0.6$ ), to reduce the likelihood of these words being skipped.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: 'Balanced across three categories' but next sentence says fillers not analyzed — adjacent contradiction

ground_truth.modified_snippet: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories.
ground_truth.description: Changed 'more varied' to 'balanced across all three categories' — contradicted by next sentence (fillers not analyzed due to low diagnosticity) and actual numbers (80 experimental vs 40 filler = not balanced)

matched_finding.subcategory: Experiment 3 fillers are not clearly verb-diagnostic
matched_finding.description: Experiment 3 fillers are not clearly verb-diagnostic: Experiment 3’s filler description appears internally inconsistent: the fillers are introduced as having suffix spellings diagnostic for verbs, but the next sentence says most verb suffixes have diagnosticity below 0.5, and Appendix A indicates that several listed suffixes are more noun- than verb-associated. Since the fillers were intended to balance sentence contexts rather than enter the main analyses, this may not affect the primary results, but the passage should distinguish syntactic-context balance from verb-diagnostic suffix cues.
matched_finding.quote: Stimuli. Eighty experimental nonwords with suffix spellings diagnostic for adjectives ( 10 suffixes) or nouns ( 10 suffixes) were selected from Experiment 1. Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5 ). The ten verb suffixes we used as fillers were -ate, -ade, -eer, -le, -yse, -ide, -our, -ice, -ure, -art.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Diagnosticity→spelling and specificity→reading, but experiments show opposite — inverts entire logic
ground_truth.original_snippet: That is, we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading), while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on spelling behaviour.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: That is, we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic cat...
ground_truth.description: Swapped diagnosticity/specificity task predictions — diagnosticity should predict reading, specificity should predict spelling; reversed mapping inverts the entire experimental logic

matched_finding.description: Reversed feedforward mapping in transition: The transition reverses the mapping between constructs and tasks. Diagnosticity is defined as spelling-to-meaning consistency and should be linked to print-to-meaning tasks; specificity is defined as meaning-to-spelling consistency and should be linked to spelling production. The subsequent Experiments section uses this opposite, conceptually correct mapping.
matched_finding.quote: In this paper, we focus solely on what is usually referred to as "feedforward" effects. That is, we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading). That said, perception and production are intertwined processes, and one might expect "feedback" effects of diagnosticity and specificity as well (e.g. diagnosticity influencing the production of spelling; see Ziegler et al., 2008; Kessler et al., 2008, for similar findings in reading aloud). This is an issue that needs to be investigated in future studies using appropriate experimental designs (e.g. a two-by-two factorial manipulation).
